content.title: About
content.content: Alfredo sauce with poultry is a creamy sauce made from heavy cream, Parmesan cheese, and butter, to which cooked chicken or turkey pieces are added. It combines a smooth, buttery flavor with a subtle hint of meat, making it a popular topping for pasta, risotto, and casseroles.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The classic Alfredo sauce was created in the early 1920s at the restaurant "Alfredo" in Rome.
The original recipe used only butter, cream, and Parmesan, without any meat.
Adding chicken or turkey became popular in the United States in the 1970s as a way to boost the protein content of the dish.
While traditionally served with fettuccine, the sauce also pairs well with whole‑grain pasta and vegetable noodles.
The creamy base can be adapted for lighter diets by substituting cream with low‑fat cottage cheese or plant‑based alternatives.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Poultry provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Calcium from Parmesan
items.content: Parmesan cheese is a good source of calcium, supporting bone and dental health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken and turkey contain vitamins B6 and B12, important for metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains vitamin D
items.content: Cream and butter contribute small amounts of vitamin D, which aids immune function.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: The fat content provides a quick source of energy, useful during high physical activity.

items.title: High fat and calorie content
items.content: The cream and butter make the sauce calorie‑dense; portion control is advised for weight management.

items.title: Lactose
items.content: Dairy ingredients contain lactose, which can be problematic for lactose‑intolerant individuals.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Parmesan and added salt increase sodium levels; people with hypertension should consume in moderation.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Those allergic to milk or cheese should choose dairy‑free versions of the sauce.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the sauce hot over pasta, rice, mashed potatoes, or vegetable gratins. Cook the poultry by boiling, roasting, or sautéing, then cut into bite‑size pieces and stir into the sauce just before finishing. Garnish with fresh herbs such as parsley or basil and a sprinkle of grated Parmesan.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared sauce in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. If freezing, the texture of the cream may change; it is best to freeze the sauce without the poultry and keep the meat separate.

content.title: About
content.content: Vault is an energy drink designed to boost focus, endurance, and rapid recovery after physical activity. It contains 200 mg of caffeine, B‑vitamins, taurine, electrolytes, and natural flavorings.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Vault uses a blend of caffeine from green coffee and guarana for a longer‑lasting effect.
Electrolytes (sodium, potassium, magnesium) are added to support fluid balance.
The drink is sugar‑free, sweetened with stevia and erythritol, making it low‑calorie.
Each 250 ml can is wrapped in aluminum foil to protect from light and preserve freshness.
Vault has undergone clinical trials on athletes, showing a 12 % improvement in reaction time.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: Caffeine and taurine stimulate the central nervous system, increasing alertness and concentration.

items.title: Metabolism support
items.content: B‑vitamins help convert carbohydrates, fats, and proteins into usable energy.

items.title: Electrolyte balance
items.content: Sodium, potassium and magnesium help prevent dehydration and muscle cramps.

items.title: Low calorie
items.content: Absence of sugar and use of sweeteners make the drink suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Green tea and guarana extracts contain polyphenols that combat free radicals.

items.title: Caffeine sensitivity
items.content: People sensitive to caffeine may experience anxiety, rapid heartbeat, or insomnia.

items.title: Not for children or pregnant women
items.content: Due to high caffeine content, the product is not recommended for children, adolescents, pregnant or nursing women.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: Caffeine can amplify the effects of certain stimulants and cold medicines.

items.title: Stomach discomfort
items.content: Some individuals may experience heartburn or gastric irritation after consumption.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Consume one 250 ml can 30 minutes before training or when energy drops. Do not exceed two cans per day. Do not mix with alcohol.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. Once opened, consume within 24 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: Idli is a traditional South Indian dish consisting of steamed cakes made from a fermented batter of rice flour and black gram (urad dal). The batter is left to ferment for 8–12 hours, then spooned into small round molds and cooked in a steamer. Idli have a soft, slightly porous texture, a neutral flavor, and are served hot with chutney, sambar, or coconut sauce.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Idli are considered one of the lightest and most nutritious foods in Indian cuisine.
They are traditionally eaten for breakfast but are enjoyed at any time of day.
Fermentation increases the bioavailability of B‑vitamins and makes the dish easier to digest.
In some regions, finely chopped vegetables such as carrots or spinach are added to the batter for color and flavor.
Idli are often served as a “triple”: one idli, a portion of sambar, and a portion of chutney.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Idli are steamed without oil, making them suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Rich in probiotics
items.content: The fermentation process promotes beneficial bacteria that support gut health.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Rice flour provides slow‑releasing energy, helping maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains plant protein
items.content: Black gram adds protein, important for tissue repair.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Idli have a lower glycemic index than plain rice, making them suitable for people with pre‑diabetes.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to black gram used in the batter.

items.title: Fermentation control
items.content: Over‑fermentation can lead to off‑flavors and the growth of undesirable microbes.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: When served with heavily salted sauces, the overall sodium intake can become high.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Idli are served hot, typically with sambar (spicy lentil stew), coconut chutney, tomato chutney, or a drizzle of ghee. They can be split and topped with butter or ghee for extra richness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cooked idli keep in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. They can be frozen for up to 1 month; reheat by steaming or microwaving before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Ruffled potato chips with cheese flavor are crunchy potato slices coated with a savory cheese seasoning. The chips are made from selected potatoes, cut into wavy slices, fried to a golden crisp, and seasoned with a blend of cheese, salt, and spices.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Ruffled chips have a larger surface area, which helps them hold more seasoning.
The cheese taste is often achieved with a mix of real cheese and flavor enhancers such as cheese powder.
The first commercial launch of cheese‑flavored chips occurred in the United States in the early 1990s.
In Russia, similar chips are popular under brands like "Lay's", "Prjany" and others.
There is a smoked‑cheese variant that gives a stronger aroma.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Potato chips provide carbohydrates that quickly supply the body with energy.

items.title: Vitamin C content
items.content: In small amounts, chips retain vitamin C, which supports the immune system.

items.title: Calcium from cheese seasoning
items.content: Cheese additives can contribute a modest amount of calcium, beneficial for bones.

items.title: Satiety satisfaction
items.content: The crunch and rich cheese flavor can promote a feeling of fullness and help curb overeating.

items.title: High sodium
items.content: The salt in the seasoning may contribute to elevated blood pressure when consumed frequently.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Chips are fried in oil, making them calorie‑dense and potentially contributing to weight gain.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Cheese seasonings contain milk proteins that can trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Trans fats in some oils
items.content: If partially hydrogenated oils are used, the product may contain trans fats.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Chips are convenient as a standalone snack, paired with dips, added to salads, or used as a crunchy topping for dishes like nachos. They should be enjoyed in moderation and balanced with healthier foods.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store chips in the original package or an airtight container in a cool, dry place away from light. Over time they may lose crunch, so it is best to consume within 2–3 months after opening.

rice-brown-with-dark-green-vegetables-an.title: Brown Rice with Dark Green Vegetables and Tomatoes/Tomato Sauce, Fat Added

content.title: About
content.content: Brown rice is a whole‑grain product that retains the bran and germ, making it more nutritious than white rice. In this dish it is combined with dark green vegetables (such as broccoli, spinach, green beans) and tomatoes or a tomato‑based sauce, plus added fat (oil or plant‑based fats) to enhance flavor and aid absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Brown rice provides more fiber, B‑vitamins, and minerals than polished white rice.
Dark green vegetables are rich in chlorophyll, giving them their characteristic color and antioxidant properties.
Tomatoes are a good source of lycopene, a carotenoid that supports protection against free radicals.
A small amount of added fat improves the bioavailability of carotenoids and vitamin K found in green vegetables.
The dish combines complex carbs, plant protein, and healthy fats, delivering sustained satiety.

items.title: Supports Digestion
items.content: Fiber from brown rice and green vegetables promotes regular bowel movements and helps prevent constipation.

items.title: Antioxidant Protection
items.content: Lycopene from tomatoes and chlorophyll from green vegetables neutralize free radicals, reducing the risk of chronic diseases.

items.title: Blood Sugar Stabilization
items.content: Complex carbohydrates in brown rice are released slowly, preventing rapid spikes in blood glucose.

items.title: Cardiovascular Support
items.content: Healthy fats and potassium from the vegetables help regulate blood pressure and improve lipid profiles.

items.title: Immune System Boost
items.content: B‑vitamins, vitamin C, and vitamin K contribute to normal immune function.

items.title: High Calorie Content
items.content: Added fat increases the dish’s energy density; portion control is advisable for those monitoring weight.

items.title: Allergy to Rice or Fats
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to rice or specific fats (e.g., nut oils).

items.title: Oxalate Content
items.content: Certain green vegetables (spinach, beet greens) are high in oxalates, which can contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot as a main course or side. Cook the rice and vegetables together, adding a splash of oil at the end of cooking. Garnish with lemon juice or fresh herbs for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Reheat with a little water or broth to prevent drying out.

content.title: About
content.content: Canned bean soup is a ready‑to‑eat product that contains beans, vegetables, spices, and broth. It stores at room temperature and heats quickly, providing a nutritious and filling meal.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Canned bean soup is popular for camping and office lunches because of its long shelf life.
Beans are a good source of plant protein, fiber, and complex carbohydrates.
Traditional recipes include tomatoes, carrots, onion, and spices such as bay leaf and black pepper.
In some countries bean soup is a national dish, e.g., feijoada in Brazil and bean soup in the United States.
Canning preserves most vitamins, though some vitamin C may be lost during heat processing.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Beans supply essential amino acids that support muscle maintenance and tissue repair.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Source of iron and magnesium
items.content: These minerals are important for hemoglobin formation and nervous system function.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Canned bean soup typically contains little saturated fat, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Convenient and economical
items.content: Quick preparation without the need to cook broth or chop vegetables saves time and money.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Canned soups often contain high levels of salt, which may be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: Bean allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beans.

items.title: Bisphenol A in packaging
items.content: Metal cans can leach trace amounts of BPA; choose products with verified safety certifications.

items.title: Thermal processing
items.content: Long‑term storage can lead to the formation of small amounts of unwanted compounds, so do not exceed the printed shelf life.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Open the can and heat the soup on the stove or in a microwave until boiling. For extra flavor, add fresh herbs, sour cream, or grated cheese.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened cans in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, transfer any leftovers to an airtight container and keep refrigerated for up to 3‑4 days.
